directAnswer: Look for a printed wattage or USB PD rating on the cable, then confirm with a USB-C power meter: 100W is USB PD 3.0 at 20V/5A; 240W is USB PD 3.1 EPR at up to 48V/5A and needs a matching EPR cable, charger, and laptop.
summary: USB-C cables are not interchangeable for high-wattage charging. Printing, e-marker chips, and a cheap inline watt meter are more reliable than color, thickness, or the fact that both ends are USB-C.

sections.heading: What 100W vs 240W actually means
sections.body: USB Power Delivery 3.0 tops out at 100W (20 volts at 5 amps). That needs a 5A cable with an e-marker chip — a 3A cable will cap you around 60W even on a 100W charger. USB PD 3.1 Extended Power Range (EPR) goes to 140W, 180W, or 240W using 28V or 48V. Those cables are physically different (EPR-marked, often thicker) and only work at those voltages with a PD 3.1 charger and a laptop that asks for EPR. A 240W cable can still charge a 65W laptop; a 60W cable cannot deliver 100W.

sections.heading: Read the cable and packaging first
sections.body: Reputable cables print 60W, 100W, or 240W on the jacket or connector. USB-IF certified cables may show the USB logo plus a wattage. Thunderbolt 4/USB4 cables are typically 5A (100W charge) but are not automatically 240W EPR cables. Charge-only or unmarked cables are often 3A (60W). Marketing like “fast charge” or a braided jacket tells you nothing.

steps.title: Check printing and the charger brick
steps.detail: Look on the cable for 60W, 100W, 140W, or 240W (or 5A / EPR). Then read the charger: PD 3.0 bricks list 20V/5A (100W); PD 3.1 EPR bricks list 28V or 48V. The weakest link wins — a 240W charger plus a 100W cable is 100W max.

steps.title: Confirm with a USB-C power meter
steps.detail: Plug a USB-C watt meter (PD tester) between charger and laptop. Charge with the lid open and the machine under load so it actually draws power. A true 100W path will show close to 20V and several amps (often 60–100W depending on the laptop). EPR/240W paths show 28V or 48V when the laptop requests them — most ultrabooks never will.

steps.title: Use the OS as a sanity check
steps.detail: On Windows, some OEM power apps or powercfg /batteryreport show charge rate, not cable rating. On Mac, System Settings → Battery can show charging watts on some machines. Phone apps that estimate current are rough and cannot prove 240W.

steps.title: Reject unmarked cables for high-wattage laptops
steps.detail: If there is no wattage print and no USB-IF/EPR marking, treat it as 60W unless a meter proves otherwise. For 100W+ laptops, buy a named 5A/100W or EPR/240W cable rather than guessing.

faqs.question: Can I tell 100W vs 240W by thickness or e-marker chips?
faqs.answer: Thickness is a hint, not a test. Both 100W and 240W cables contain an e-marker. 240W / PD 3.1 EPR cables are specified for higher voltage and must be marked for EPR — a normal 100W 5A cable is not 240W.

faqs.question: My laptop only charges at 60W with a 100W charger. Is the cable the problem?
faqs.answer: Often yes: a 3A cable limits PD to 60W (20V/3A). Also check that you are on the laptop’s full-power USB-C port (some ports are lower wattage) and that a dock is not sitting in between.

faqs.question: Do I need a 240W cable for a 100W laptop?
faqs.answer: No. A certified 100W (5A) cable is enough. 240W cables are for PD 3.1 laptops and chargers that actually negotiate 28V/48V.

caveats: A meter reading of 45W or 65W does not mean the cable is 45W — many laptops simply do not draw 100W while idle.
Never assume a USB-C cable is safe at 5A because it fits. Cheap unmarked cables can overheat.
